skills.name: Name methods of soil conservation
skills.mastery: The child names terracing (steps on a slope), contour farming, mulching, cover crops, planting trees and strip cropping, and says they slow water and wind so soil is not carried away. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 6 controlled erosion on slopes; Grade 8 names the conservation measures. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Laying a structure across the slope came with retention ditches in Grade 7. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how soil conservation measures are laid out and built on a slope
skills.mastery: Says how soil conservation measures are carried out: mark the contour (with an A-frame or line level), lay stone lines or trash lines along it, build soil bunds with the soil thrown uphill or downhill as designed, plant strips of crops or grass across the slope, grass a waterway to carry extra water safely, and repair after heavy rain; in the app the child picks the right step, order, tool, material or reason in new situations. The practical (carrying out soil conservation activities in the school) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child names the measures before carrying them out. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks terraces speed up water running down a slope.

example.question: What does terracing do on a slope?
example.correct_answer: Slows the water and holds soil

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the steps and pictures water falling down them faster.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Speeds up the water" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Pour water down a tray with and without small steps of soil; time it.
misconceptions.feedback: Terraces slow water and hold soil.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks mulch leaves the soil bare.

example.question: What does mulch do to soil?
example.correct_answer: Covers and protects it

misconceptions.cause: The child confuses mulching with clearing the land.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Leaves it bare" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Lay mulch on a tray and show it covering the soil from raindrops.
misconceptions.feedback: Mulch covers and protects soil.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Ploughs and plants up and down the slope.

example.question: How should crops be planted on a slope?
example.correct_answer: Along the contour

misconceptions.cause: Straight rows up the slope look neat and are easy to walk.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Up and down the slope" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Recall Grade 6: rows across the slope stop water; rows down the slope become channels.
misconceptions.feedback: Plant along the contour.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Burns crop trash instead of laying it in trash lines.

example.question: What can be done with maize stalks after harvest to conserve soil?
example.wrong_answer: Burn them to clear the field
example.correct_answer: Lay them in lines across the slope as trash lines

misconceptions.cause: Burning is the usual way to clear fields and the child does not see the trash as a tool.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Burn them to clear the field" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a trash line holding soil behind it after rain.
misconceptions.feedback: Lay crop trash in lines across the slope. It traps soil and rots into manure.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lays stone lines by eye, so they slope and water runs along them to one end.

example.question: How is a stone line laid on a slope?
example.correct_answer: Along a contour marked with an A-frame or line level

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks "across" is close enough.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "By eye, roughly across" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour water along a tilted line on a model; it runs to the low end and cuts a gully.
misconceptions.feedback: Mark the contour first so the line is level and water spreads, not runs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a grassed waterway should be left bare so water flows freely.

example.question: Why is a waterway planted with grass?
example.correct_answer: Grass holds the soil while the water flows over it

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks water needs a clear channel.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "So it looks nice" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Run water down a bare channel and a grassed channel on a model.
misconceptions.feedback: Grass in a waterway holds the soil so the flowing water does not cut a gully.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks strip cropping means planting strips running down the slope.

example.question: How are strips laid out in strip cropping?
example.correct_answer: Across the slope, alternating crops with grass or cover crops

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures strips as straight rows in any direction.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Down the slope" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw both on a slope and trace where rain water goes.
misconceptions.feedback: Strips go across the slope so each strip catches soil washed from the one above.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks bunds and stone lines last for ever without repair.

example.question: What must be done to soil bunds after a heavy storm?
example.correct_answer: Check and repair breaks

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks building is the end of the job.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a broken bund with a gully below the break.
misconceptions.feedback: Check and repair bunds after storms. One break lets all the water through.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves stored water uncovered.

example.question: How should stored water be kept?
example.correct_answer: In a clean, covered container

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks water is clean as long as it looks clear.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Uncovered" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Leave a basin of water uncovered for two days; look at the dust, insects and larvae.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep water covered.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Drinks harvested rain water untreated because rain is pure.

example.question: What should be done before drinking harvested water?
example.correct_answer: Boil or purify it

misconceptions.cause: The child knows rain falls clean and forgets the roof, gutters and tank.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Show the dirt washed off a roof in the first rain.
misconceptions.feedback: Boil or purify before drinking.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a tank is covered only to keep the water warm.

example.question: Why must water tanks be covered?
example.correct_answer: To keep out dirt and mosquitoes

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link open water with mosquitoes breeding.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "To warm the water" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Show mosquito larvae in an open container; malaria mosquitoes breed in still water.
misconceptions.feedback: Covers keep out dirt and mosquitoes.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Stores drinking water in old chemical or fuel containers.

example.question: Which container is safe for storing drinking water?
example.correct_answer: A clean container used only for water

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks washing removes all traces.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "An old paraffin jerrycan" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Smell a washed paraffin can.
misconceptions.feedback: Use containers made and kept only for water. Chemical and fuel cans stay unsafe.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lets the first dirty rain from the roof go straight into the tank.

example.question: What is done with the first rain from a roof?
example.correct_answer: Let it run away, then collect the cleaner water

misconceptions.cause: The child does not want to waste any water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Let it into the tank" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Collect the first and the later rain in two glasses and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Let the first flush wash the roof and run away. Collect the cleaner water after it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Fixes gutters flat or sloping away from the tank.

example.question: How must a gutter be fixed?
example.correct_answer: Sloping gently towards the down pipe and tank

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks water flows along any gutter.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Flat along the roof" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour water into a flat gutter model: it stands and overflows.
misconceptions.feedback: Gutters slope gently towards the down pipe so water flows to the tank.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Fits the tank tap at the very bottom.

example.question: Why is the tank tap fitted a little above the bottom?
example.wrong_answer: It should be at the very bottom
example.correct_answer: So the dirt that settles at the bottom does not come out

misconceptions.cause: The child wants to use every drop.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It should be at the very bottom" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Let muddy water settle in a bottle; which layer would a bottom tap draw?
misconceptions.feedback: Fit the tap above the bottom so the settled dirt stays in the tank.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Never cleans the roof, gutters or tank.

example.question: How often should gutters and the tank be cleaned?
example.correct_answer: Before the rains and regularly after

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks rain cleans the system.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Never" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show leaves and mud from a blocked gutter.
misconceptions.feedback: Clean the roof, gutters and tank before the rains and regularly after.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

prepare a kitchen or backyard garden and plant various crops such as vegetables, herbs and spices,

sub_strands.pcis: Poverty eradication as learners establish their garden to grow own foods.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate growing of own food in kitchen and backyard garden to financial literacy skills learnt in Pre-Technical Studies.

skills.name: Explain the role of a kitchen and backyard garden

skills.mastery: Says how a kitchen or backyard garden is established: a site near the house and water with sun, fenced, beds or a keyhole garden prepared with manure, a mix of vegetables, herbs and spices planted in small, staggered amounts for a steady supply, watered with saved water, weeded and harvested often; in the app the child picks the right step, order, tool, material or reason in new situations. misconceptions.error: Thinks a kitchen garden must be on a large farm far from the house.

example.question: Where is a kitchen garden kept?
example.correct_answer: Near the house

misconceptions.cause: The child links growing food with big fields.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "On a distant large farm" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Show a keyhole garden two steps from a kitchen door.
misconceptions.feedback: A kitchen garden is near the house.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Names timber trees or maize as crops for a kitchen garden.

example.question: Which crop suits a kitchen garden?

misconceptions.cause: The child lists any plants grown at home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Timber trees" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the cook needs every day: greens, onions, tomatoes, herbs.
misconceptions.feedback: Sukuma wiki suits a kitchen garden.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a kitchen garden costs a family more than buying vegetables.

example.question: How does a kitchen garden help a family?
example.correct_answer: It saves money on vegetables

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It costs a lot more" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Count the shillings spent on sukuma wiki in a month against a packet of seed.
misconceptions.feedback: It saves money.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a kitchen garden grows just one crop in a large amount.

example.question: What is grown in a kitchen garden?
example.wrong_answer: One crop in a large amount
example.correct_answer: A small mix of vegetables, herbs and spices

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures a farm field of one crop.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "One crop in a large amount" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a kitchen garden plan with many small patches.
misconceptions.feedback: A kitchen garden grows a little of many crops the family uses often.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Plants all the vegetables on the same day, so they are ready together and then nothing.

example.question: How can a kitchen garden give vegetables all the time?
example.correct_answer: Plant small amounts every two or three weeks

misconceptions.cause: The child does not plan ahead for a steady supply.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Plant everything on one day" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a harvest calendar for one planting and for staggered plantings.
misconceptions.feedback: Plant small amounts every few weeks so there is always something to harvest.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Sites the garden far from the house and water.

example.question: Where is a kitchen garden best placed?
example.wrong_answer: Far from the house in the shade
example.correct_answer: Near the house and water, in the sun

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks gardens belong away from homes.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Far from the house in the shade" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask how often the cook goes to pick greens, and how water is carried.
misconceptions.feedback: Put the kitchen garden near the house and water, in the sun.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the garden unfenced among chickens and goats.

example.question: Why fence a backyard garden?
example.correct_answer: To keep chickens, goats and other animals out

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks home animals will not eat the garden.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not needed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a bed scratched by chickens.
misconceptions.feedback: Fence the garden so home animals do not eat or scratch it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks herbs and spices cannot be grown at home.

example.question: Which herb can be grown in a kitchen garden?
example.wrong_answer: None, herbs come only from shops
example.correct_answer: Dhania, mint or rosemary

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None, herbs come only from shops" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Grow dhania in a tin in class.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Designs a waterer that cannot be opened or cleaned.

example.question: Why must a waterer be easy to clean?
example.correct_answer: Slime and germs build up inside and must be washed out daily

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks closed means clean.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It does not need cleaning" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Look inside a sealed waterer after a week.
misconceptions.feedback: Design the waterer so it opens and can be washed daily.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Starts building before naming the problem with the old waterer.

example.question: What is the first step in designing an innovative waterer?
example.correct_answer: Name the problem with the existing waterer

misconceptions.cause: The child is keen to make something.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Start building" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List the problems found on the household visits.
misconceptions.feedback: Start by naming the problem. The design must solve it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: discuss and share experiences on how ICT can be used to access supplies and information for appropriate decision making,

access online platforms for ICT support services such as weather forecast, veterinary services, supply services, extension services, market information and banking services, catering services, cleaning services.
discuss and adhere to responsible use of ICT platforms by observing ethical and security considerations.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we access support services using ICT?
sub_strands.core_competences: Digital literacy: digital citizenship skills as learners access online platform for ICT support services.
sub_strands.values: Integrity: ethical use of online support services.
sub_strands.pcis: Cyber security: This is developed as the learners observe online security guideline to prevent cyber-attacks.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate the access of ICT support services to digital technology skills learnt in Pre-technical Studies.

outcomes.text: describe support services that can be accessed through use of ICT
access support services using ICT
show responsibility in use of ICT in accessing support services

skills.name: Describe support services reached through ICT
skills.mastery: The child names eCitizen, M-Pesa, online lessons, farm advice and weather SMS as services reached through a phone or computer, and says they are used safely with a trusted adult. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the right answer in a short story
find the false step in a learner's reason

prerequisites.reason: Pre-Technical Grade 7 named ICT tools and what each is used for. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Online threats from Pre-Technical Grade 7 are why ICT services are used responsibly. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how a support service is reached safely through ICT
skills.mastery: Says how to access an ICT support service (weather forecast, veterinary or extension advice, market prices, supplies, banking, catering or cleaning services) by SMS, USSD code, app or website: find the right official service, follow the steps, check the information against another source, keep PINs and passwords private, and log out; in the app the child picks the right step, order, tool, material or reason in new situations. The practical (accessing support services using ICT with the teacher) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child knows which services exist before accessing one. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Protecting data on a device (Pre-Technical Grade 8) keeps PINs and passwords safe. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Names a service that does not use ICT, such as a bus ride, as an ICT service.

example.question: Which service is reached through ICT?
example.correct_answer: eCitizen

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks any service people pay for is an ICT service.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A bus ride" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: An ICT service is reached through a phone, computer or the internet: eCitizen, M-Pesa, weather SMS.
misconceptions.feedback: eCitizen is an ICT service.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a weather forecast by SMS is of no use to a farmer.

example.question: How can a weather SMS help a farmer?
example.correct_answer: It tells when rain is likely

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks weather cannot be known in advance.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It cannot help" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Ask when a farmer should plant, spray or harvest; a forecast helps choose the day.
misconceptions.feedback: It helps plan farm work.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Shares a PIN or password with friends or callers.

example.question: What should you do with your password?
example.correct_answer: Keep it private

misconceptions.cause: The child trusts friends and people who sound official.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Share it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new situation.
misconceptions.help: Real services never ask for your PIN. Keep it private; tell an adult about such calls.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep passwords private.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by an Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a farmer can get vet or extension advice only by travelling to an office.

example.question: How can a farmer get advice about a sick cow without travelling?
example.correct_answer: Through a phone helpline, SMS or app service for farmers

misconceptions.cause: The child has not seen advice given by phone.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is no way" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a farmer helpline or SMS service with the teacher.
misconceptions.feedback: Farmers can get vet and extension advice by phone, SMS or app.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Trusts any message or website that claims to be a service.

example.question: An SMS says you have won a prize and asks you to send money to claim it. What is it?
example.wrong_answer: A real service; send the money
example.correct_answer: A scam; do not reply and tell an adult

misconceptions.cause: The child trusts official-sounding messages.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A real service; send the money" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a real service message with a scam message.
misconceptions.feedback: Real services do not ask you to send money to claim a prize. Do not reply; tell an adult.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Acts on market price information from one source without checking.

example.question: Why check market price information with another source?
example.correct_answer: Prices change and one source can be wrong or old

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks anything on a phone is true.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not needed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare prices from two services for the same day.
misconceptions.feedback: Check information with a second source before you act on it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves an account open on a shared computer.

example.question: What should you do after using an online service on a shared computer?
example.correct_answer: Log out

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks closing the window ends the session.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Just close the window" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show how the next user can open the account after the window is closed.
misconceptions.feedback: Always log out of online services on a shared computer.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Dials random codes hoping to reach a service.

example.question: How do you find the right USSD code or number for a service?
example.correct_answer: Use the official code from the provider or a trusted source

misconceptions.cause: The child guesses instead of looking up.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Try any code" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show where official codes are printed: posters, the provider's website.
misconceptions.feedback: Use only official codes and numbers from the provider.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
